Piercing.text: Flesh Puncture: The point slips through skin and fat, leaving a narrow bleeding hole.
Muscle Nick: The point enters muscle. The wound clenches around it and blood wells steadily from the track.
Tendon Graze: A tendon or ligament is scored. The limb catches painfully when flexed.
Nerve Puncture: The point catches a peripheral nerve. The limb burns, tingles, spasms, or goes partly numb.
Joint Penetration: The point enters a joint capsule. Blood and synovial fluid seep from a deep, exquisitely painful wound.
Organ Puncture: The weapon enters the torso and perforates a hollow or solid organ. Much of the bleeding is where no one can see it.
Major Vessel Puncture: A deep vessel is opened. Blood pulses or pours into flesh, chest, abdomen, or open air.
Eye Destroyed: The point ruptures the globe and enters the orbit. The eye collapses in blood and vitreous fluid.
Punctured Lung: Lung and pleura are penetrated. Blood and air fill the chest as the lung collapses.
Transfixing Vital Wound: The point passes through neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, or spinal canal, tearing major vessels and organs in its path.
Vital Transfixion: Heart, great vessels, brainstem, or another indispensable structure is completely penetrated. Death is immediate.

Slashing.text: Nick: Skin opens in a thin red line. It stings more than it harms.
Skin Flap: A shallow slice lifts skin and fat from the body. Blood sheets across the wound.
Shallow Gash: The edge passes through skin into superficial muscle, leaving a broad wound that pulls open with movement.
Deep Laceration: Muscle fibres are divided. The wound gapes and fills rapidly with blood.
Tendon Laceration: The blade partly severs tendon or ligament. The affected hand, foot, or joint moves weakly and unnaturally.
Nerve Severed: A deep cut divides muscle and a major peripheral nerve. Distal flesh goes weak, numb, or useless.
Muscle Belly Split: A major muscle is opened nearly to the bone. The cut contracts apart into a wet red trench.
Arterial Laceration: A major artery is opened. Bright blood jets with the heartbeat and rapidly pools around the victim.
Traumatic Amputation: A hand, foot, forearm, lower leg, or comparable part is severed or left attached by scraps of tissue.
Disembowelment: The abdominal wall is laid open; bowel, mesentery, and torn viscera spill through the wound amid massive internal and external hemorrhage.
Decapitation: The neck is severed through vessels, airway, spine, and cord. Death is immediate.

Bludgeoning.text: Bone Rattle: The blow lands solidly. Flesh throbs and the struck bone rings with deep pain.
Hematoma: Small vessels rupture beneath intact skin. The area swells purple-black and becomes exquisitely tender.
Simple Fracture: A bone cracks without gross displacement. Weight or leverage produces sickening movement and pain.
Rib Fracture: One or more ribs break. Every breath, cough, twist, or impact drives the fragments against injured tissue.
Dislocation: A joint is violently forced out of articulation. The limb hangs at the wrong angle until reduced.
Concussion: The brain is violently accelerated inside the skull. Vision swims; memory skips; nausea and confusion follow.
Ruptured Organ: A spleen, liver, kidney, or similar organ tears and bleeds internally beneath unbroken skin.
Spinal Fracture: Vertebrae fracture or displace, injuring nerve roots or spinal cord. Weakness, numbness, or paralysis follows below the injury.
Crush Injury: Bone, muscle, vessels, and nerves are pulverized together; a pelvis, limb, or chest wall deforms under the blow.
Massive Polytrauma: Multiple bones shatter; chest, pelvis, spine, and internal organs fail together under overwhelming force.
Skull Crushed: The skull collapses and brain tissue is destroyed. Death is immediate.

Shot.text: Bullet Graze: The projectile ploughs a bloody furrow through skin without remaining in the body.
Soft-Tissue Passage: The shot passes through flesh, leaving a permanent wound track and ragged bleeding openings.
Muscle Channel: The projectile tears through muscle; tissue around its path is bruised, stretched, and shredded.
Bone Strike: The shot clips bone, gouging cortex and driving fragments into surrounding flesh.
Joint Shot: The projectile enters a joint, breaking articular bone and scattering fragments through cartilage, tendon, and capsule.
Comminuted Fracture: Bone bursts into several fragments; bullet and bone splinters tear through adjacent muscle, vessels, and nerves.
Visceral Gunshot: The projectile crosses chest or abdomen and perforates lung, bowel, liver, spleen, kidney, or another major organ.
Major Vessel Shot: A large artery or vein is torn by projectile, bone, or fragments. Internal or external hemorrhage becomes immediately catastrophic.
Shattered Limb: Bone and soft tissue are catastrophically disrupted; the extremity may be unsalvageable even if still attached.
Devastating Torso Shot: Projectile and fragments cross multiple vital structures, producing massive hemorrhage, destroyed organs, and a ragged wound channel through the body.
Central Destruction: The shot destroys the brain, upper spinal cord, heart, great vessels, or an equivalent volume of indispensable tissue. Death is immediate.

Shocking.text: Paresthesia: A violent tingling snap runs through the nerves. Fingers twitch and skin prickles after contact ends.
Muscle Spasm: Current forces involuntary contraction. Jaw, hands, or limbs clamp and release painfully.
Contact Burn: Electrical energy cooks small patches of skin while nerves fire chaotically beneath them.
Neuropraxia: A nerve temporarily stops conducting normally. A limb becomes numb, weak, clumsy, or briefly useless.
Arc-Blast Rupture: The blast ruptures an eardrum and leaves the victim deafened, dizzy, and disoriented.
Deep Muscle Injury: Current passes through muscle, producing tetany, swelling, deep thermal injury, and occult tissue necrosis.
Cardiac Arrhythmia: The heart's rhythm becomes unstable. The victim collapses as beats flutter, race, or cease momentarily.
Rhabdomyolysis: Large volumes of muscle die and swell; dark myoglobin floods the blood and threatens the kidneys.
Cardiorespiratory Arrest: Current crossing chest or brain arrests breathing, heartbeat, or both before spontaneous circulation returns.
Massive Electrical Trauma: Deep muscle and nerve necrosis, vascular injury, arrhythmia, compartment damage, and organ failure occur along the current path.
Thunderbolt: Massive current destroys cardiac, respiratory, and nervous function at once. Death is immediate.

Burning.text: Superficial Burn: Skin reddens, swells, and becomes painfully hypersensitive.
Blistering Burn: Partial-thickness injury raises clear blisters over raw, intensely painful skin.
Deep Partial-Thickness Burn: Deeper dermis is destroyed; the wound is mottled red and white, wet, swollen, and exquisitely painful.
Full-Thickness Patch: Skin is destroyed through its full depth, becoming pale, waxy, brown, or black. The centre may be strangely numb.
Circumferential Burn: Deep burned tissue encircles a limb or torso, swelling beneath an unyielding eschar and threatening blood flow or breathing.
Deep Full-Thickness Burn: Destruction extends through skin into subcutaneous fat. Dead tissue sloughs and fluid pours from the wound.
Muscle and Tendon Burn: Heat or caustic action penetrates fascia, muscle, tendon, and vessels; living flesh contracts away from dead tissue.
Destroyed Extremity: An extremity is charred, cooked, or chemically necrosed beyond functional recovery.
Extensive Burn Shock: A large portion of the body is deeply burned; fluid loss, swelling, inflammation, and circulatory collapse threaten every organ.
Massive Full-Thickness Burns: Great sheets of skin and deeper tissue are destroyed. Shock, airway injury, infection, and multiorgan failure follow.
Complete Immolation: Destructive heat or caustic force consumes the body beyond survival. Death is immediate.

Toxic.text: Nausea: Stomach rolls, mouth waters, and the world feels subtly wrong.
Paresthesia: Skin crawls, burns, itches, or goes numb as the agent reaches peripheral nerves and tissues.
Systemic Malaise: Feverish weakness, headache, chills, tremor, and aching muscles spread through the body.
Violent Purging: Vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, salivation, or other uncontrolled secretions rapidly dehydrate the victim.
Coagulopathy: The blood no longer clots properly—or clots where it should not. Bruising blooms beneath the skin and blood leaks from gums, nose, gut, or wounds.
Neurotoxic Weakness: Motor nerves fail progressively. Muscles weaken, coordination disappears, and paralysis begins at the extremities.
Respiratory Depression: Breathing becomes slow, shallow, irregular, or mechanically impossible as respiratory muscles or brainstem drive fail.
Hepatorenal Injury: Liver or kidneys begin to fail under the toxic burden; metabolites and cellular debris accumulate in the blood.
Toxic Shock: Circulation collapses amid arrhythmia, seizures, hypoxia, or overwhelming systemic inflammation.
Multiorgan Collapse: Nervous system, circulation, respiration, liver, and kidneys fail together. The body can no longer clear the poison or sustain itself.
Toxic Arrest: Respiration, circulation, or cellular metabolism fails irreversibly. Death is immediate.

Freezing.text: Frostnip: Skin reddens or pales and burns with sharp cold before becoming numb.
Numbed Extremity: Fingers, toes, ears, or exposed flesh become waxy and insensate; fine movement turns clumsy.
Superficial Frostbite: Frozen skin becomes pale and firm; rewarming brings violent pain and clear blistering.
Deep Frostbite: Injury extends beneath skin. Hemorrhagic blisters form after thawing and the tissue becomes blue-purple and swollen.
Frozen Joint: Tendons, capsule, and surrounding tissue stiffen and freeze; movement becomes painful, weak, and mechanically unreliable.
Hypothermic Confusion: Core temperature falls enough to impair judgement, speech, memory, and coordination. Shivering becomes violent or begins to fail.
Deep Tissue Freezing: Ice injury and microvascular thrombosis kill muscle, nerve, and vessels beneath deceptively intact skin.
Frozen Extremity: A hand, foot, or larger part freezes deeply. After thawing it darkens toward necrosis and may ultimately require amputation.
Severe Hypothermia: Consciousness fades and the heart becomes dangerously irritable; pulse and breathing slow toward arrest.
Profound Cold Injury: Core hypothermia and widespread frozen tissue produce coma, arrhythmia, circulatory failure, and irreversible tissue death.
Flash-Frozen: Vital tissues freeze or core temperature collapses beyond survival in moments. Death is immediate.

panic.text: Euphoria: Terror becomes exhilaration. Gain [+] on your next player-facing roll.
Self-Doubt. You are certain you cannot do this. Your next Attack or Ability Check is [–].
Tunnel Vision. The world narrows to the thing before you. Your next AC Save is [–].
Hesitation. Your feet refuse the order your mind gives them. Lose your next Move.
Fumble. Your hands betray you. Drop your active weapon, Artifice, or tool; if you hold none, lose your next Action.
Flinch. You recoil at the worst possible instant. Lose your next Action.
Breathless. Your chest tightens; every breath comes short and ragged. Halve your Move until the immediate danger ends.
Tremors. Your hands shake and fine control deserts you. Attacks, Ability Checks, and opposed rolls are [–] until the immediate danger ends.
Cry Out. Terror tears a shout from you before you can choke it back. Lose your next Action and scream. Resolve the noise normally.
Freeze. For a terrible heartbeat, you simply cannot move. Lose your next Action and Move.
Recoil. Instinct overwhelms discipline. You throw yourself toward safety. Spend your next Action and Move Running toward the safest available cover or ally, away from the threat.
Overwhelmed. Thought collapses into one command: get out. For 1d4 Rounds, you may only retreat, take cover, or directly help yourself or another escape.

Cower. Something inside you gives way. Release held items and fall Prone. For 1d4 Rounds, you cannot Act or Move. An adjacent companion may spend an Action to bring you back to yourself, ending this early.
Flight. You bolt. Formation and orders forgotten. Run from the source of Panic for 1d4 Rounds, taking the safest apparent route you can see.
Shutdown. Your mind simply refuses what your senses are telling it. You stare, curl up, or go rigid. Become Out for 1d4 Rounds.
Hysterics. Terror bursts loose uncontrollably. You scream, sob, laugh, pray, or babble. Become Out for 1d4 Rounds, loudly.
Rout. Courage breaks completely. Release held items and Run until clear of immediate danger. You cannot willingly return to that danger until Relief or Revelry reduces your Stress.
Collapse. Your strength leaves you. Whether fainting, retching, shaking, or staring blankly, you are finished for now. Become Out for 1d6 dungeon Turns.
Unresponsive. The horror reaches somewhere deep and shuts the door behind it. You cannot be reasoned with, roused, or made useful. Become Out for 1d6 hours.

Broken. Something in you finally snaps. You collapse into stupor, delirium, desperate prayer, or senseless terror and cannot simply be ordered back onto your feet. Become Out until you complete a Safe Rest with care and reduce Stress through Relief or Revelry.

rows.text: Two workers from 80 call through the upper grille and lower a rope for an announced arrival.
The trolley rolls toward the litter turn: catch its trailing brake rope, wedge the wheel or clear the lane; impact 2d6 Bludgeoning.
Web quivers at the lower door. One mineral-flue spider from 22 can reach 25 via RR009 to 24, RR100 to 23, RR016 to 21 and RR157 to 25 if those cargo doors stand open.
A tattered stretcher cover at the rest bears NORTH LIGHT and the date of the retreat. The footprints run down toward 25.
Two P10 from 136 descend after passing 137–132–144 by RR070, RR188 and RX120. Their hooks test the next door; deduct them from the reserve while absent.
A fibre trembles across the rooted upper drain. Cutting it interrupts the warning link but alerts the connected centre to the break.
The flood shutter moves toward a litter. Its handwheel and a pole under the braced leaf can hold the gap.
A carrier from 144 brings an empty rope basket for a lost tool. Help at the last bend earns a lamp fill from that crew’s carried supplies.
Two P10 from 195’s reserve descend with empty harness straps. Iron scrapes around the bend before the soldiers reach it.
A severed carrying strap releases its hanging hook toward the path: support it or clear the line; impact 1d6 Bludgeoning.
The upper root draws a bloodstained rag through the shutter slit. The motion reveals the drain holding its chain.
A reserve scout’s return passes the rest door. Its lamp, armament and burden follow its preceding journey; a shut rest door hides those sheltering inside.
Two P10 from 206’s five reserves bring an empty sled down. Their ropes occupy the narrow bend before they see the company.
The lower fire door swings shut behind a carrier. A wedge or a scout through its drain can keep the return open.
Edmund Marr’s borrowed voice speaks through a root beside the stair. It asks after a name remembered by the dead king; cutting that branch silences it here.
A retreating 206 patrol climbs toward the upper firing rest, calling for the loading-house door. Blocking the rest denies its defenders that cover.
Two waterkeepers descend from the south draw carrying a sealed sample. They ask for a lamp while crossing a dark rest.
A calf-sized wild animal rattles the closed crop vent. A P15 skyserpent reaches through a hand-sized grille for the lamp’s insect cloud.
Two hose workers from 135 haul a replacement line up. Their coil blocks the bend until somebody holds the outer loop.
Fresh bootmarks end at the last latched reserve compartment. A barred door separates those listening inside from the passing company.
Two Crown Watch carriers descend from 214 with dressings. They know which bedside holds the two wounded from Bourne’s failed rescue.
A loose counterweight swings into its recess, throwing grit across the next tread. Stop outside the sweep or brace it; impact 2d6 Bludgeoning.
At the lower mouth, one P10 from 195 tests the defended tap gate. It enters the stair only after that gate is opened or overrun; the waterkeepers call from the wall.
A waterkeeper climbs with a tap report. Escorting the report to 214 earns a meal; the messenger will take a night watch beside a supplied company.
